claims.overstatement: None in the part of the claim that comes from this source; the claim reports the study's sample, recall design, small effect sizes, age dependence and the authors' conclusions accurately. Three precision points are in the note.
claims.note: Checked against this source: Project MATCH 1991–1993, nine sites; 379 women and 1,210 men with all four landmark ages, recalled at baseline; arm × gender × current-age-quintile ANOVA with nothing else adjusted for; landmark ages 2.5 to 3.9 years later in women (26.6 vs 22.7, 27.5 vs 25.0, 29.8 vs 27.2), worst period 35.2 vs 35.0; intervals 0.9 vs 2.3, 2.3 vs 2.2, 5.5 vs 7.8 with all SDs as printed; 735 first-treatment people, 11.6 (9.01) vs 15.8 (9.67), F(1, 715) = 44.5; ω² .01 to .04; youngest quintile mean age 26.6, drunk regularly 18.8 vs 18.0, oldest 37.8 vs 30.7; 53% in the assumed order; entry ages 38.3 to 41.7 (Table 1); the authors' 'relatively robust' conclusion (abstract) and their recommendation to alert women (p. 259). Editors' arithmetic reproduced: 3.9 (26.6 − 22.7), 4.2 (15.8 − 11.6), Table 2 quintile gaps 0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1, 7.1; my own pixel reading of Figure 1 gives men vs women 8.0/7.2, 13.1/11.1, 16.2/11.7, 18.9/11.2, 25.0/18.5, gaps about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7 and 6.5 years, so 'about 0.8 to 7.7' is right. Precision points: (1) the 'same entry ages' (38 to 42) are Table 1 ages at trial entry for all 1,589; ages by sex for the 735 first-treatment people are not reported, and the 3.9-year gap (Table 2, 1,589 people) and the 4.2-year gap (735 people) come from different samples, so 'editors' comparison' should stay labelled as approximate. (2) 'Grew with age' is shown by Gender × Age interactions for three landmark ages and for time to first treatment; no such interaction is reported for the two shorter intervals, and the Results (p. 255) and Discussion (pp. 257–258) disagree on whether the loss-of-control interaction was significant (F = 3.32 with 4 and 1,569 df gives p ≈ .010, not ≤ .001 as printed; my calculation). (3) The study did not ask ages at first drink or first intoxication (p. 258), so it says nothing about time from first use, which the claim's opening frames; the claim correctly starts the intervals at getting drunk regularly. No dosing or advice content.

anchors.extracted: Project MATCH enrolled 1,307 men and 419 women seeking treatment for alcohol problems, recruited over 2 years, 1991 to 1993, at nine US clinical research units; outpatient arm 688 men and 264 women (community via newspaper advertisements and outpatient programmes), aftercare arm 619 men and 155 women (inpatient or day-hospital programmes). DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence, age 18 or over; current dependence on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana, suicidality and psychosis excluded.

Landmark ages taken at the baseline assessment on entry to the trial: age at first alcohol-related problems and at onset of the worst period from the SCID interview; age at first getting drunk regularly and at first difficulty stopping drinking to intoxication (loss of control) from two self-administered DrInC items. 1,589 of the 1,726 enrolled gave all four ages and form the analysis sample.

Landmark ages, intervals between successive landmarks (differences of recalled ages in the average order, so negative values possible) and time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment (only where MATCH was the first treatment) analysed by 2 (arm) × 2 (gender) × 5 (current-age quintile) between-subjects ANOVA; no covariates. Mean (SD) current age per quintile 26.6 (2.92), 33.2 (1.42), 38.2 (1.61), 44.3 (2.13), 56.9 (6.34).

Analysis sample by sex and arm: women aftercare n 148, age 41.7 (SD 12.17); women outpatient n 231, 38.3 (10.70); men aftercare n 576, 41.5 (10.68); men outpatient n 634, 38.5 (10.51); age differences flagged for arm only, not sex; 96% to 98% alcohol-dependent in each cell. Ages by sex for the 735 first-treatment people are not given.

Women (n 379) vs men (n 1,210), mean (SD) age: drunk regularly 26.6 (10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96); first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87); loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95); worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93). Gender F(1, 1,569) = 83.62, 32.35 and 38.67 for the first three (p ≤ .001), ω² = .03, .01, .01; differences 2.5 to 3.9 years, called small relative to total variation but clinically meaningful. No gender difference for worst problems (Discussion, p. 258).

anchors.locator: Results › Age-of-onset data, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, age-quintile rows
anchors.extracted: Gender × Age Quintile F(4, 1,569) = 6.81 (drunk regularly), 4.37 (first problems), 3.32 (loss of control), ω² .01 each: gender differences minor or absent in the youngest quintile and larger with age; quintile 1 drunk regularly 18.8 vs 18.0, quintile 5 37.8 vs 30.7. F = 3.32 printed p ≤ .001 gives p ≈ .010 (my calculation), and the Discussion (pp. 257–258) calls this interaction non-significant.

anchors.locator: Results › Order of landmark events, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: On average the landmarks came in the order drunk regularly, first problems, loss of control, worst problems (mean within-person ranks 1.6, 2.0, 2.7, 3.7), but only 53% of individual participants reported this pattern.

anchors.locator: Results › Progression through successive landmark events, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 3
anchors.extracted: Women vs men, mean (SD) years: drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04), gender F(1, 1,569) = 13.04, ω² .01; first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), no significant effect; loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67), gender F = 20.95 (df printed 1/1,589), ω² .01.

anchors.locator: Results › Progression from drunk regularly to first treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: MATCH was the first reported treatment for 735 people. Time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment, women 11.6 (SD 9.01) vs men 15.8 (9.67) years; gender F(1, 715) = 44.5, ω² .04; age quintile F(4, 715) = 48.41, ω² .17; Gender × Age F(4, 715) = 3.76, ω² .01; no significant gender difference in the youngest quintile, significant in the other four. Numbers of women and men among the 735 not reported.

Mean time from drunk regularly to first treatment by sex and quintile (735 people; no cell sizes or SDs). My reading at 300 dpi, men vs women: 8.0/7.2, 13.1/11.1, 16.2/11.7, 18.9/11.2, 25.0/18.5 years; gaps about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7, 6.5, close to the gaps in age at getting drunk regularly in Table 2 (0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1, 7.1; full 1,589).

Ages at first drink and first intoxication were not asked; similar results for first problems to first treatment are asserted without data. Younger participants entered treatment after similar intervals regardless of sex; the authors offer either a subset of fast progressors or changed norms as explanations and cannot choose between them.
Authors conclude telescoping is a relatively robust phenomenon in treatment-seeking alcoholics and that women are more likely to progress faster through the landmarks.

Authors grant the differences are small relative to total variation, call them clinically meaningful, and say women should be alerted that they are more likely than men to develop alcohol problems and dependence relatively rapidly; the next paragraph limits the conclusions to the Project MATCH sample.

key_findings.note: All numbers match. Minor locator detail: the nine clinical research units are in the 2nd paragraph of Method › Subjects (Inclusion/exclusion criteria), not the 1st.
χ² = 4.97 with 1 df gives p ≈ .026 (my calculation), as the note says.
Standardized differences recomputed with pooled SD: 0.42, 0.25, 0.25, 0.02.
My independent pixel measurement of Figure 1 at 300 dpi gives 8.02/7.21, 13.09/11.10, 16.18/11.67, 18.88/11.16, 24.95/18.47.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed p ≈ .010; with the univariate α of .05/4 = .0125 the interaction would still pass the univariate test, which may explain the Results; the Discussion's 'no significant interaction' remains inconsistent.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence fits a descriptive comparison of women and men in one sample; overall high for the site's question is right (selection at treatment entry ties intervals ending at treatment to recruitment age; recalled ages; small effects absent in the youngest).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'relatively robust' and the advice to alert women in general go beyond small, age-confined effects in a treatment sample.

missed: p. 258, Discussion, 5th paragraph: the questionnaire did not ask ages at first drink or first intoxication, so this study cannot speak to time from first use to problems or treatment (the framing used by Piazza et al. and by the claim's opening sentence). Worth a key finding.

p. 256 with p. 253: 'first treatment' for the 735 is MATCH itself, but aftercare-arm participants were recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes, and how that index episode was counted is not stated; minor, affects which arm contributes to the 735.
